concepts.title: Learner state
concepts.summary: Mastery tracking and a personalized path through the graph.
concepts.overview: Learner state covers mastery tracking and a personalized path through the graph. A prerequisite graph describes the subject, and learner state describes where one person currently stands in it. The survey finds this mostly in systems built for teaching. [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) and [PathFinder](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S) track it, and PathFinder uses [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/01M3VX5JTF73ZNZ625SBW6M4Y8) and replans when quiz scores arrive. Code-graph and wiki tools such as [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) have none. One design lesson is that mastery should come from a transparent model, either BKT or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites (see [Encompassing edges and implicit credit](#c/01M3VX5JTF78BF5A42144QBYEP)), and not from LLM judgment. Of the four pillars, this is the one the reader marked as only a nice-to-have.

concepts.title: Adoption / health
concepts.summary: Stars, recent commits and maintainers: is the project alive enough to build on?

overviewProv.quote: Stars, recent commits, maintainers

concepts.overview: Adoption and health asks whether a project is alive enough to build on: how many stars it has, whether commits are recent, and whether anyone maintains it. It is one of the criteria in [What we need from a tool](#c/01M3VX5JTFWPV5M0HJVQG2QEC8), and the research reads it as a practical filter. [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) has the cleanest data model but was archived in 2023. [Learn Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF02V8JNS4TVP0AFZ7) is effectively discontinued as open source. [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) has good ideas but 1★. [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) meets the bar easily, with about 40k★ and releases every few days. The pattern is that adoption lies with tutors and code-graph tools, while the best prerequisite designs are small or dead.

concepts.title: Sigma.js
concepts.summary: WebGL renderer that handles thousands of nodes: the whole-field "map of knowledge" scale.

overviewProv.quote: WebGL, handles thousands of nodes (a whole-field "map of knowledge")

concepts.overview: Sigma.js is a WebGL graph renderer (about 12.2k★) that can draw thousands of nodes. In this Expedition that makes it the candidate for the zoomed-out, whole-field "map of knowledge", where other libraries would slow down. The report pairs it with Cytoscape.js as a choice for the learner view, alongside a dagre or ELK layered layout. It is one of the [Visualization building blocks](#c/01M3VX5JTF86GCRSS10AP3HP15). It supports [Visualize DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P), which wants a view that zooms from one target concept up to the whole field. The report lists it as a library and does not test it.

concepts.title: Concept graph with prerequisites
concepts.summary: Knowledge split into well-defined chunks, with typed directed "you need A before B" edges (ideally a validated DAG), not just "related to" links.

overviewProv.quote: Edges say *"you need A before B"*.
Typed, directed "requires" edges (ideally a validated DAG), not just "related to" links

concepts.overview: This is the first and most fundamental thing the Expedition asks of a tool: knowledge split into well-defined chunks, joined by typed, directed edges that say "you need A before B". The Sources insist on a real prerequisite model, ideally a validated DAG, rather than loose "related to" links, because only then can a learner be given an ordered plan. It rests on [chunked nodes](#c/01M3VX5JTF7GMZBF7H9N2DCAEA), since edges need self-contained units to connect, and it is refined by [distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD). The survey shows it is the pillar where data-model projects such as [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28), [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) and [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) shine. The popular tutors like [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) and [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) fail it, and [LLM Wiki](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV) offers only untyped links.

sections.heading: What counts as a prerequisite model?
sections.md:
The rubric asks for **typed, directed "requires" edges, ideally a validated DAG, not just "related to" links**. The nodes must also be self-contained learning units (see [chunked nodes](#c/01M3VX5JTF7GMZBF7H9N2DCAEA)), because an edge like "you need A before B" is only useful if A and B are well-defined chunks.

The payoff is a computed learning order. [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) shows it: pick a target concept and it lists every unmet prerequisite in topological order, each with curated resources. A loose web of related links cannot give you that plan.

sections.heading: Who meets it, and how
sections.md:
Several projects have the right data model, each in a different form:

- [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28): concepts that point to their prerequisites, plus curated resources and time estimates.
- [Learning Commons Knowledge Graph](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G): learning progressions, the Math Coherence Map and a curriculum dependency endpoint for K-12.
- [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T): `\uses{}` records dependencies, and a statement and its proof carry separate dependency lists.
- [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H): every edge cites evidence from the source texts.
- [PathFinder](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S): a hand-built skill DAG in NetworkX, validated for cycles.
- [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7): strong, but only for code, where dependencies can be extracted mechanically.
- [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVR82GYYSAK21HNY): typed, directed links such as `requires`, built from frontmatter.

[Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) meets it only partly: lessons declare prerequisite skills, but there is no full graph. [Graphify](#c/01M3VX5JTFDRBN32X7KNR8FXDD) and [roadmap.sh](#c/01M3VX5JTFCR3JQRMANXC178KZ) are also partial, because their edges are general relations or roadmap order rather than strict prerequisites.

sections.heading: Who fails it
sections.md:
The most popular tools mostly fail this criterion:

- [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) uses knowledge graphs inside retrieval, with no curated, learner-visible prerequisite graph.
- [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) produces a linear course outline, not a graph.
- The [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV) has links only. Typed `prerequisites:` frontmatter would take it most of the way.
- [STORM / Co-STORM](#c/01M3VX5JTF1F4074GEG6NM1A17) keeps a hierarchy, not prerequisites.
- [GraphRAG and agent-memory tools](#c/01M3VX5JTFZB7W8YXQQ7YNGGC9) extract entity and relation graphs and do not model "learn A before B".

sections.heading: Why the edges are hard to get right
sections.md:
Prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and errors cost most. On K12-Bench prerequisite reasoning, Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match. A missing or backwards prerequisite sends a learner into material they cannot yet follow.

History shows the other side of the problem. Metacademy's downfall was the **curation bottleneck**: experts had to hand-write every node and edge.

The Sources suggest several refinements:

- Use [distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD): `requires`, `helps`, `part-of`, `related`, `encompasses`.
- Consider depth-qualified prerequisites, such as "requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*".
- Validate the structure automatically. [OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform](#c/01M3VX5JTFT71WC90C5DSQF0XV) runs CI checks for duplicate ids, broken references and prerequisite cycles.
- Where a vetted graph exists, [reuse it](#c/01M3VX5JTFTBA6PQJEN5GGYSBG) instead of regenerating it.

sections.heading: DAGs, not trees
sections.md: Prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees. That is why tree-shaped mind-map tools, which are easy LLM output targets, cannot express them. For viewing, a layered (Sugiyama) layout with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top reads far better than a force-directed one for the question "what do I need first?".

concepts.title: Visual exploration
concepts.summary: A learner can see where a concept sits, what it depends on and what it unlocks; a graph/map, not just a list.
concepts.overview: Visual exploration means a learner can see where a concept sits, what it depends on, and what it unlocks, through a graph or map and not just a list. It is one of the reader's hard requirements. Tools that stop at a list or outline fail it: [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) has no learner-facing concept map and [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) offers a linear outline. [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) and [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) meet it with rendered dependency graphs and overview-to-detail zoom. Prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees, so a layered layout with foundations at the bottom reads better than a force-directed one. This is the reasoning behind [Visualize DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P). The practical options are libraries such as [Cytoscape.js](#c/01M3VX5JTFF04PQ6EN5ZP4955B) and Sigma.js.

concepts.title: Built-in LLM / agent capabilities
concepts.summary: The LLM generates nodes, proposes edges, writes explanations, tutors and checks mastery.
concepts.overview: This criterion asks whether a tool uses an LLM or agents to generate nodes, propose edges, write explanations, tutor, and check mastery. The tools in the survey vary widely on it. [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) predates LLMs and [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) has no LLM authoring of its graph. [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H), [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) and [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) have strong agent capabilities. Strong LLM support is easy to find, though, and it does not solve the real problem. The research shows that [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9), so agent output has to be treated as a proposal. That is why this criterion works together with [Human + LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE): the LLM supplies volume, and a person decides what is accepted.

concepts.title: Human + LLM co-curation
concepts.summary: A person reviews, edits and approves what the LLM proposes, with provenance, review/approve workflow and versioning.

overviewProv.quote: A person reviews, edits, and approves what the LLM proposes, with provenance.

concepts.overview: Co-curation is the fourth pillar: a person reviews, edits and approves what the LLM proposes, and the result keeps provenance and version history. It matters here because LLMs are unreliable at judging prerequisites, so a machine-generated graph needs a human in the loop before learners rely on it. It depends on [built-in LLM capabilities](#c/01M3VX5JTETAKFAMQZ3G4CDG5Y), since there must be proposals to review. The Sources show it working in different forms: [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) has humans and AI working in parallel on nodes, [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) lets people edit an outline before generation, and the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV) uses plain files and git diffs. GraphRAG-style tools offer none of it.

sections.heading: What the criterion asks for
sections.md: The rubric calls for a **review/approve workflow, direct editing, provenance and versioning**. A person must stay in charge of what the LLM proposes. The question is whether the tool makes that practical, not whether it merely allows it.

sections.heading: Why a human has to stay in the loop
sections.md:
The evidence is the weak showing of LLMs as prerequisite judges. Frontier models score only about 46–57% exact match on K12-Bench.

Research also shows how to spend expert time well. **ACE** scores concept pairs, sends only the top-ranked candidates to experts, and infers more edges from what the experts confirm. That cut expert effort a lot, and students who studied in ACE's order had better success rates. The Sources call it the blueprint for a review queue. **Concept Catalyst** takes a gentler route: teachers build the concept map while the LLM stays behind the interface as a suggestion generator, so decisions stay with the teacher.

sections.heading: Patterns that already work
sections.md:
Several tools show the pattern in different forms:

- [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T): small, locally specified nodes let many humans and AI agents work in parallel, and global progress is a roll-up of node statuses.
- [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6): a human-editable outline before generation, plus "Edit with AI" using validated JSON-patch edits.
- [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV): plain files, git and an agent governed by a schema file. The human reads and edits in Obsidian.
- [roadmap.sh](#c/01M3VX5JTFCR3JQRMANXC178KZ): one markdown file per node, changed by community PRs. This proves file-per-node curation works at scale.
- [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7): a separate graph-reviewer agent, and a graph committed as JSON so teams share it.
- [STORM / Co-STORM](#c/01M3VX5JTF1F4074GEG6NM1A17): a human joins the agents' discussion around a shared mind map.

sections.heading: Where tools fall short
sections.md:
Co-curation is partial or absent in some places:

- [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) was expert-edited only, with no LLM proposals to review.
- [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) has an independent critic model, but its human audit is still pending.
- [GraphRAG and agent-memory tools](#c/01M3VX5JTFZB7W8YXQQ7YNGGC9) offer no curation at all.
- The weekend [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVR82GYYSAK21HNY) route has git diffs for review, but lacks a shared review workflow.

sections.heading: What the Expedition takes from this
sections.md: The design implication is to make every edge a **proposal** carrying a confidence score and cited evidence. Low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a human review queue, and the tool records who approved what. Keeping the content in plain files under version control means agents and humans edit the same files and review happens in diffs or PRs.

concepts.title: What we need from a tool
concepts.summary: The four pillars the reader wants and the rubric used to judge every tool.
concepts.overview: This topic holds the reader's four pillars and the rubric the survey used to judge each tool. The pillars are a [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z), [Visual exploration](#c/01M3VX5JTETK31MX1A5D8ZDA40), [Built-in LLM / agent capabilities](#c/01M3VX5JTETAKFAMQZ3G4CDG5Y), and [Human + LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE). The rubric adds four more criteria: self-contained [Chunked nodes](#c/01M3VX5JTF7GMZBF7H9N2DCAEA), [Learner state](#c/01M3VX5JTEDCGXQKK50HVQ13QK), [Adoption / health](#c/01M3VX5JTEXKJVCZ6TR1EKDH31), and a [Buildable license](#c/01M3VX5JTFP4W4JWDEP8ET8PEM). Together they frame [Which open-source tools already do most of this?](#c/01M3VX5JTFXZFZYQA25MQKFFH3). They also explain the conclusion in [No tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV), because each tool is scored against these same criteria.

concepts.title: Prerequisite graphs & mastery systems
concepts.summary: Tools with the right data model: concepts joined by "you need A before B" edges, plus learner state and curation.
concepts.overview: This is the family of tools whose data model matches what the reader wants: concepts joined by "you need A before B" edges, often with learner state and curation on top. [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) computes a personalized learning plan by listing all unmet prerequisites in topological order. [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) uses prerequisite skills to drive review questions. [Learning Commons Knowledge Graph](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G) supplies vetted K-12 prerequisite data. Many small projects, such as [PathFinder](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S), add Bayesian mastery tracking. The family has the right structure but little or no LLM co-authoring and weak visualization. Metacademy's downfall was the [Curation bottleneck](#c/01M3VX5JTFEKMXGWF0CT69D643): experts had to write every node and edge by hand.

concepts.title: AI tutors & course generators
concepts.summary: Hugely adopted LLM teaching tools that generate lessons and quizzes but have no curatable prerequisite graph.

overviewProv.quote: they have **no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph**.

concepts.overview: This topic collects the AI tutors and course generators that dominate open-source adoption in 2026: [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) at about 40k stars and [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) at about 39k. It also includes the "learn from your sources" tools [Open Notebook and Khoj](#c/01M3VX5JTF1T7X67V897QK3QFD) and the [closed-source references](#c/01M3VX5JTFCQE7M1Y1BWC18FEK). These tools generate lessons, quizzes and mastery paths, so they supply the LLM and agent capability the Expedition wants. What they lack is an explicit, curatable prerequisite graph: knowledge graphs appear only inside retrieval, or the course is a linear outline. Read them as the "how to teach" layer that a curated concept DAG could direct, since the graph decides what comes next and the tutor teaches it.

concepts.title: LLM-built graphs & curation patterns
concepts.summary: Tools and patterns where an LLM builds a graph or wiki and a human reviews it: code graphs, LLM Wiki, Co-STORM.

overviewProv.quote: LLM knowledge curation covers Karpathy's LLM Wiki pattern and Stanford's Co-STORM.

concepts.overview: This topic groups the tools and patterns in which an LLM builds a graph or wiki and a human stays in the loop to read, edit and correct it. It covers code-focused tools such as [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) and [Graphify](#c/01M3VX5JTFDRBN32X7KNR8FXDD), Karpathy's [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV), and Stanford's [STORM / Co-STORM](#c/01M3VX5JTF1F4074GEG6NM1A17). They matter here because they supply the co-curation half of the goal: they show the UX of an LLM-built graph with a guided tour, and the workflow of plain files, git and an agent governed by a schema. None of them models prerequisites for general knowledge, though. Their structures are code dependencies, wikis or mind-map hierarchies, which is why this topic feeds the finding that [no tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV).

concepts.title: Infrastructure & DIY tooling
concepts.summary: GraphRAG and agent-memory substrates, and note-taking tools that could host a weekend prototype.
concepts.overview: Infrastructure and DIY tooling covers two things the Expedition treats as substrate rather than finished answers. The first is [GraphRAG and agent-memory tools](#c/01M3VX5JTFZB7W8YXQQ7YNGGC9), which extract entity and relation graphs for retrieval. They don't model learning order and their graphs are noisy for teaching, but they could find candidate concepts in a corpus. The second is note-taking software, chiefly [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVR82GYYSAK21HNY) and [Other PKM tools (InfraNodus, Logseq, AFFiNE)](#c/01M3VX5JTF8VPBXXTKZXEDC2AH). Together with an LLM agent they make the [Weekend DIY prototype](#c/01M3VX5JTFV1MWZTC2B13GNJN7) possible, which reaches about 70% of the vision for one user. It lacks a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and a shared review workflow.

concepts.title: Visualization building blocks
concepts.summary: Libraries for drawing and editing the graph, and how a prerequisite DAG should be laid out.

overviewProv.quote: Prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**.

concepts.overview: Visualization building blocks are the libraries you would use to draw and edit a concept graph. The research sorts them by job. [React Flow (xyflow)](#c/01M3VX5JTFSD3KMM3VHWHF88BP) suits an editable curation interface. [Cytoscape.js](#c/01M3VX5JTFF04PQ6EN5ZP4955B) brings graph algorithms and layered layouts such as dagre. [Sigma.js](#c/01M3VX5JTE8Y75GAH3M40GXHRZ) renders thousands of nodes in WebGL for a whole-field map. [Mind-map and canvas libraries](#c/01M3VX5JTFZVBHPJKN85302YAF) are easy LLM output targets but cannot express a DAG. The key design point, captured in [Visualize DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P), is that prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees, so a layered layout with foundations at the bottom reads better than a force-directed one.

concepts.title: Research evidence
concepts.summary: Papers showing why LLM prerequisite edges need human review and how to structure that review.
concepts.overview: Research evidence gathers the papers behind the Expedition's main design choices. The central finding is in [K12-KGraph / K12-Bench](#c/01M3VX5JTF20PV52WBR4MQQCMR): frontier LLMs reach only about 46–57% exact match on prerequisite reasoning, which is the core of [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9). The remedy comes from [ACE (AI-assisted educational KG construction)](#c/01M3VX5JTFBP36DDQ7PBZTN44P), which ranks candidate edges, sends only the top ones to experts and infers more from their confirmations, cutting expert effort. [Concept Catalyst](#c/01M3VX5JTF0F3ZQP2FA5MHBCZH) keeps decisions with teachers, and [Other research on concept and prerequisite extraction](#c/01M3VX5JTFY9BC1T1EJY48PH0G) covers related work. Together they justify a human review queue.

concepts.title: Design implications & build plan
concepts.summary: What the survey implies for building the missing tool, and a suggested starting stack.
concepts.overview: This topic gathers what the survey implies for anyone building the missing tool. The central design points are these: make every edge a proposal with evidence and confidence ([Edges are proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX)), use several edge types ([Use distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD)), keep content in files under version control ([Plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE)), and keep the curated graph apart from the tutor ([Keep graph separate from tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF)). It also advises reusing vetted graphs, shipping as an agent skill or MCP server, and visualizing DAG-first. The material ends in a concrete [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC). Two open questions remain on the topic: how to model depth-qualified prerequisites, and how to build graphs beyond K-12, code and math.

concepts.title: Which open-source tools already do most of this?
concepts.summary: None does all four pillars well; the space splits into groups each covering one or two. Best models to copy: Lean Blueprint, roadmap.sh, Oppia/PathFinder, SyllabusGraph, Understand-Anything.

overviewProv.quote: No open-source project does all four well today.

concepts.overview: This is the question the whole Expedition answers: is there already an open-source tool that gives you a concept graph with prerequisites, visual exploration, built-in LLM help, and human review of what the LLM proposes? The survey's verdict, developed in [No tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV), is no. The field splits into families that each cover one or two pillars. [Prerequisite graphs & mastery systems](#c/01M3VX5JTFYK1K1Y3CQN0PE0BK) have the right data model but little LLM help. [AI tutors & course generators](#c/01M3VX5JTFZPDYGDKAV1GBXVBR) have the LLM and the adoption but no curatable prerequisite graph. Code-graph tools such as [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) show the right user experience, but only for codebases. The question matters because the answer decides whether you adopt something or build your own. The report points to models worth copying, such as [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) and [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H).

sections.heading: The four pillars behind the question
sections.md:
The question tests tools against four pillars:

1. A concept graph with prerequisites.
2. Visual exploration, so a learner sees where a concept sits, what it depends on and what it unlocks.
3. Built-in LLM or agent capabilities to generate nodes, propose edges, explain, tutor and check mastery.
4. Human and LLM co-curation, with provenance.

The rubric adds four more checks: chunked nodes, learner state, adoption/health and whether the license lets you build on it.

sections.heading: The answer: no single tool, five families
sections.md:
The survey's verdict is that no open-source project does all four well today. The space splits into five groups, each covering one or two pillars:

- **Prerequisite-graph learning systems** ([Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28), [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK), [Learning Commons](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G), small DAG engines). They have the right data model, with little or no LLM co-authoring and weak visualization.
- **AI tutors and course generators** ([DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) at about 40k stars, [OpenMAIC](#c/01M3VX5JTFBAX0QG1P4PCZSDK6) at about 39k). They have huge adoption, but no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph.
- **Code graphs that teach** ([Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7), [Graphify](#c/01M3VX5JTFDRBN32X7KNR8FXDD)). They have the right user experience, but for codebases rather than general knowledge.
- **LLM knowledge curation** (the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV), [Co-STORM](#c/01M3VX5JTF1F4074GEG6NM1A17)). Human and LLM co-build a wiki or mind-map hierarchy, not a prerequisite DAG.
- **GraphRAG infrastructure**. It extracts entity and relation graphs for retrieval, with no pedagogy.

The comparison matrix shows the same pattern: nothing scores strongly across all four columns.

sections.heading: Which tools to copy
sections.md:
The report recommends borrowing a pattern from each:

- **Curation and data format:** [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T), a typed dependency graph with per-node status.
- **Git-based content:** [roadmap.sh](#c/01M3VX5JTFCR3JQRMANXC178KZ) and [Learn Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF02V8JNS4TVP0AFZ7), one markdown file per node, changed by PR.
- **Learner modeling:** [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) and [PathFinder](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S), prerequisite skills plus Bayesian Knowledge Tracing.
- **Evidence-backed extraction:** [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H), where every edge cites a source and an independent critic reviews the graph.
- **UX for "LLM builds a graph, then gives a guided tour":** Understand-Anything.

License matters when choosing what to build on. roadmap.sh has a restrictive custom license, so you can study it but not build on it.

sections.heading: What fills the gap?
sections.md:
The "opening" the survey identifies is a local-first, git-backed concept DAG. An agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence. A human accepts or rejects them in a review queue. Learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. The survey finds nothing mature and open that fills this slot.

For someone with limited time, a weekend prototype on Obsidian with the Breadcrumbs plugin and an LLM-Wiki-style agent can reach roughly 70% of the vision for a single user. It lacks a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and a shared review workflow.

concepts.title: Chunked nodes
concepts.summary: Nodes are self-contained learning units with content (explanation, resources, checks).

overviewProv.quote: Nodes are self-contained learning units with content (explanation, resources, checks)

concepts.overview: Chunked nodes is the criterion that each node be a self-contained learning unit, with an explanation, resources and checks, not just a label. It is part of [What we need from a tool](#c/01M3VX5JTFWPV5M0HJVQG2QEC8) and comes first logically, since you need well-defined chunks before you can draw "A before B" edges, as [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z) assumes. [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) offers a battle-tested granularity: a skill is phrased as "given X, compute Y" and carries a concept card, worked examples and misconceptions. [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) shows the collaboration payoff: small, locally specified nodes let many humans and AI agents work in parallel.

concepts.summary: Can you build on it? Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0) pass; custom, AGPL, mixed or commercial-only terms need checking.

overviewProv.quote: Can you build on it?

concepts.overview: Buildable license asks a blunt question: can you build on this tool? Permissive licenses such as MIT and Apache-2.0 pass, which is why [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) (Apache-2.0) counts as a safe foundation. Others fail. It is part of [What we need from a tool](#c/01M3VX5JTFWPV5M0HJVQG2QEC8), and mixed, AGPL or commercial-only terms need checking before any build, as [License traps](#c/01M3VX5JTFD490GQFTHTSJ20XE) describes.

concepts.title: Build a curatable learning concept DAG
concepts.summary: A local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges, a human reviews them, and learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays.
concepts.overview: This is the goal the Expedition builds toward: a curatable learning concept DAG that is local-first and git-backed. An agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges, a human reviews them, and learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. It exists because [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P) shows nothing mature fills this niche. The design needs several ingredients drawn from the Sources: [distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD), [plain files plus git](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE), a [review queue for proposed edges](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4), [DAG-first visualization](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P), and a graph kept [separate from the tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF). The [suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC) sketches a concrete route.

sections.heading: What would the finished thing look like?
sections.md:
The Sources describe the opening as a **local-first, git-backed concept DAG**. An agent *proposes* nodes and prerequisite edges, each with evidence and a confidence score. A human accepts or rejects them in a review queue. Learners then explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. The Sources conclude that nothing mature and open fills this slot, which is the gap in [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P).

The goal is to combine four things that today live in separate projects: a prerequisite model, visual exploration, LLM help, and human co-curation.

prov.quote: a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent *proposes* nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence

sections.heading: How should the content be stored and typed?
sections.md:
Content lives in **plain files under version control**: one markdown file per concept, with frontmatter for prerequisites, objectives, resources and checks. Agents and humans edit the same files, and review happens in diffs or pull requests. CI checks for cycles and dangling references keep the DAG valid. See [plain files plus git](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE).

Edges should be typed rather than a single "related to" link. The Sources suggest:

- `requires`: a hard prerequisite
- `helps`: a soft prerequisite
- `part-of`: decomposition
- `related`
- `encompasses`: Math Academy-style implicit practice

They also suggest considering *depth-qualified* prerequisites, such as requiring B at the "apply" level and not only at "define". This is the point of [distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD).

sections.heading: How do humans and agents share the work?
sections.md:
Prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and where errors cost the most. A missing or backwards prerequisite sends a learner into material they cannot yet follow. So every edge is a **proposal** carrying a confidence score and cited evidence, and low-confidence or high-impact edges go to a [review queue](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4) where approvals are recorded.

The suggested agent split is a proposer that extracts concepts and edges with citations, a critic that checks cycles, missing prerequisites and evidence, and a tutor that handles per-node explanation and quizzes. The curated DAG decides *what* to learn and in what order, and the tutor handles *how*. This is the principle of keeping the [graph separate from the tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF). Mastery should come from a transparent model such as BKT or credit flowing to prerequisites, not from LLM judgment.

sections.heading: How should learners see it?
sections.md: Visualization should be [DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P). Prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees, and a layered (Sugiyama) layout with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top reads far better than a force-directed one for "what do I need first?". The learner view should show a layered plan for one target concept and zoom out to a whole-field map. Mastery is overlaid on top, and AI-proposed edges that have not been reviewed are drawn in a distinct style.

sections.heading: What is a practical route to building it?
sections.md:
The [suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC) is a folder of `concepts/*.md` files with `requires`, `helps`, `status: proposed|reviewed` and `confidence` in the frontmatter. It adds a React Flow curation UI with an accept/reject queue and a Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js learner view with dagre/ELK layout. Seed data could come from Learning Commons for K-12, or from a user corpus run through a LightRAG/Graphify-style ingestion pass.

Two further suggestions from the Sources are to reuse vetted graphs where they exist rather than regenerate them, and to distribute the work as an agent skill or MCP server plus a static viewer, as Graphify and Understand-Anything did.

concepts.title: Review queue for proposed edges
concepts.summary: A React Flow editor with accept/reject queue for proposed edges; git commits record provenance. Status per concept: proposed or reviewed, plus confidence.

overviewProv.quote: React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges. Git commits record provenance.

concepts.overview: The review queue is the curation interface proposed for the starting stack: a React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges, where git commits record who approved what. Each concept carries a status of proposed or reviewed plus a confidence value, so low-confidence or high-impact edges can be routed to a person first. The pattern comes from ACE, which scored concept pairs, sent only the top-ranked candidates to experts and inferred more edges from their confirmations, cutting expert effort sharply. It depends on [edges being proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX), since the reviewer needs the confidence and citations on screen. The queue is part of the wider [curation UI](#c/01M3VX5JTFPW48SYXWGQXZYPKG), and it directly addresses the curation bottleneck that sank Metacademy.

concepts.title: Learn Anything
concepts.summary: Began 2017 as community-curated mind maps and learning paths; the repo now holds a different dormant project (Linsa), so effectively discontinued as open source.

overviewProv.quote: now holds a **different, dormant project (Linsa)**, so this is effectively discontinued as open source

concepts.overview: Learn Anything is a historical reference. It began in 2017 as open-source, community-curated mind maps and learning paths, later billed as AI- and community-guided. Its repository (16.9k★) now holds a different, dormant project called Linsa, so it is effectively discontinued as open source. It is useful as evidence that community-curated learning maps attracted people but did not stay healthy, and it fails the [Adoption / health](#c/01M3VX5JTEXKJVCZ6TR1EKDH31) criterion. The report groups it with other [Prerequisite graphs & mastery systems](#c/01M3VX5JTFYK1K1Y3CQN0PE0BK) and cites it, with roadmap.sh, for the pattern of one file per node changed by pull request.

concepts.title: Math Academy
concepts.summary: Closed-source; probably the best product built on a prerequisite graph. Hand-curated topic graph with "encompassing" edges giving implicit review credit to prerequisites, plus diagnostic placement.

overviewProv.quote: It uses a hand-curated topic graph with "encompassing" edges

concepts.overview: Math Academy is a closed-source product that the report calls probably the best existing one built on a prerequisite knowledge graph. It relies on a hand-curated topic graph with "encompassing" edges: practicing an advanced topic gives implicit review credit to its prerequisites. It also offers diagnostic placement. Its main lesson for this Expedition is [encompassing edges and implicit credit](#c/01M3VX5JTF78BF5A42144QBYEP), which feeds a transparent mastery model. Because it is closed, it fails the [buildable license](#c/01M3VX5JTFP4W4JWDEP8ET8PEM) test and can only be studied, not reused. It belongs to the group of [prerequisite graphs and mastery systems](#c/01M3VX5JTFYK1K1Y3CQN0PE0BK).

concepts.title: Open Notebook and Khoj
concepts.summary: Open-source NotebookLM alternatives for chat, sources and podcasts (Open Notebook ~39.4k★ MIT, no mind maps; Khoj ~37.5k★ AGPL-3.0, Mermaid mind maps). A "learn from your sources" layer, not graph tools.

overviewProv.quote: Relevant as a "learn from your sources" layer, not as graph tools.

concepts.overview: Open Notebook (~39.4k★, MIT) and Khoj (~37.5k★, AGPL-3.0) are open-source alternatives to NotebookLM, offering chat over your sources, and podcasts. Open Notebook has no mind maps; Khoj can produce Mermaid mind maps. The report treats them as a "learn from your sources" layer, not graph tools, so they fail the [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z) criterion. They belong to [AI tutors & course generators](#c/01M3VX5JTFZPDYGDKAV1GBXVBR), which have large adoption but no curatable prerequisite structure. For this Expedition they matter as popular companions to a curated graph, not as candidates to build it on.

concepts.title: OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform
concepts.summary: One curriculum.json (tracks → modules → skills → lessons) with CI checks for duplicate IDs, broken references and prerequisite cycles; zoom/pan graph view; changes by PR.
concepts.overview: OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform is a tiny project (0 stars) worth reading for its engineering habits rather than adoption. All its content lives in one curriculum.json, organised as tracks, modules, skills and lessons, with a graph view that supports zoom and pan. Its notable idea is continuous-integration checks that fail on duplicate IDs, broken references and prerequisite cycles, and changes arrive by pull request. This is direct evidence for the claim that [plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE): agents and humans edit the same files, and automated checks keep the graph a valid DAG. It belongs with the other small [prerequisite graph and mastery systems](#c/01M3VX5JTFYK1K1Y3CQN0PE0BK).

concepts.title: Other small DAG and mastery engines
concepts.summary: Tiny projects worth reading for ideas: propositional-logic "Math Academy" (fractional credit to prerequisites), Skillgraph_OS (prerequisite vs helps-with edges), math-concept-mapper (class prerequisite gaps), Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine, niyue/skillmap.

overviewProv.quote: All are tiny (0–1★). They are worth reading for design ideas, not for adoption.

concepts.overview: This is a set of tiny prerequisite DAG and mastery projects (0–1★) that the report values for patterns, not adoption. Examples include a propositional-logic "Math Academy" that gives fractional credit to prerequisite topics, and Skillgraph_OS, which separates "prerequisite" from "helps-with" edges and supports alternative routes. Others are math-concept-mapper, with class-wide prerequisite gaps, Cognitive-knowledge-graph-engine, and niyue/skillmap, a text DSL for skill trees. Skillgraph_OS directly supports [using distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD). As a group they illustrate that the [best patterns come from tiny projects](#c/01M3VX5JTFB8BRJK63TSVKWP1M). They belong to the wider field of [prerequisite graphs and mastery systems](#c/01M3VX5JTFYK1K1Y3CQN0PE0BK).

concepts.title: Other PKM tools (InfraNodus, Logseq, AFFiNE)
concepts.summary: InfraNodus finds clusters and gaps between them (AGPL plugin, commercial backend); Logseq is an outliner with graph view (AGPL, ~45k★); AFFiNE is local-first docs+whiteboard with AI (~73k★, mixed license).

overviewProv.quote: mixed license (check before building on it)

concepts.overview: This group covers three personal-knowledge-management tools that could serve the DIY route. InfraNodus AI Graph View, an Obsidian plugin, analyzes text networks to find topical clusters, central ideas and gaps between clusters. The plugin is AGPL-3.0 but its backend is a commercial SaaS. Logseq is an open-source outliner with graph view and whiteboards (AGPL-3.0, ~45k★). AFFiNE is local-first docs, whiteboard and mind map with AI features (~73k★, mixed license). None models prerequisites directly. Because of the AGPL and mixed terms, they are examples of [License traps](#c/01M3VX5JTFD490GQFTHTSJ20XE), and the report says to check AFFiNE before building on it. They sit in [Infrastructure & DIY tooling](#c/01M3VX5JTF9H6P45YCX9PC1WGF) beside the Obsidian route.

concepts.title: Other closed-source references
concepts.summary: For comparison only: Khan Academy (old knowledge map retired; Khanmigo tutor), NotebookLM (hierarchical auto mind maps, hard to edit), Heptabase/Scrintal/Kosmik (human-built card whiteboards), InfraNodus SaaS.
concepts.overview: These are commercial products the research looked at only for comparison, since none of them can be built on. The most relevant is [Math Academy](#c/01M3VX5JTFDNTBN42YTX9C9XJT), which sits in the same group and is probably the best existing product on a prerequisite knowledge graph. The rest show what is missing from the open side. Khan Academy retired its old knowledge map of exercises and now offers the Khanmigo LLM tutor. NotebookLM auto-generates mind maps from sources, but they are hierarchical rather than prerequisite-based and hard to edit. Heptabase, Scrintal and Kosmik are card whiteboards where the human draws the map. InfraNodus is commercial text-network analysis. Because they are closed source they fail the [Buildable license](#c/01M3VX5JTFP4W4JWDEP8ET8PEM) test. They sit within [AI tutors & course generators](#c/01M3VX5JTFZPDYGDKAV1GBXVBR) as reference points, not options.

concepts.title: React Flow (xyflow)
concepts.summary: Best fit for an editable node/edge UI (curation); pair with ELK or dagre for layered DAG layout.
concepts.overview: React Flow, published by the xyflow project, is a library with about 38.5k stars. The research picks it as the best choice for an editable node-and-edge interface, which is what human curation needs. It does not compute layouts for layered prerequisite graphs itself, so it is paired with ELK or dagre to place foundations below and goals above. In the suggested stack it powers the [Curation UI](#c/01M3VX5JTFPW48SYXWGQXZYPKG), where reviewers accept or reject proposed edges. For learner-facing exploration the same stack uses Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js instead, so React Flow's role is editing rather than whole-field viewing. It is one of the [visualization building blocks](#c/01M3VX5JTF86GCRSS10AP3HP15) compared in the research.

concepts.title: Cytoscape.js
concepts.summary: Graph algorithms plus many layouts, including dagre and klay for prerequisite DAGs; suited to the learner-facing view.

overviewProv.quote: Graph algorithms plus many layouts, including `dagre` and `klay` for prerequisite DAGs

concepts.overview: Cytoscape.js is a graph library (~11.2k★) that combines graph algorithms with many layouts, including `dagre` and `klay`, which suit prerequisite DAGs. The report recommends it, or Sigma.js, for the learner-facing view in the suggested stack. That view should be [DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P): a layered layout with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top, which reads better than force-directed layouts for "what do I need first?". Its algorithms also help with paths and mastery overlays. [React Flow](#c/01M3VX5JTFSD3KMM3VHWHF88BP) covers the editable curation side.

concepts.title: Mind-map and canvas libraries
concepts.summary: markmap (13.1k★) and simple-mind-map (12.8k★) make tree mind maps from markdown, an easy LLM output target but unable to express a DAG. Excalidraw (133k★) and tldraw (51k★) are freeform canvases; tldraw needs a commercial license for production.

overviewProv.quote: Tree-shaped mind maps from markdown. Easy LLM output target, but can't express a DAG

concepts.overview: This group covers two kinds of freeform visual tools: tree mind-map libraries and canvas editors. markmap (13.1k★) and simple-mind-map (12.8k★) turn markdown into tree-shaped mind maps. They are an easy target for LLM output, but a tree cannot express a DAG, and prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees. That limit supports [Visualize DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P). Excalidraw (133k★) and tldraw (51k★) are freeform canvases where a human draws the structure. tldraw needs a commercial license for production use, which makes it an example of [License traps](#c/01M3VX5JTFD490GQFTHTSJ20XE). The group belongs to [Visualization building blocks](#c/01M3VX5JTF86GCRSS10AP3HP15) but fits the learner-facing graph worse than the layered options.

concepts.title: Suggested starting stack
concepts.summary: The report's proposal, not a validated design: concepts/*.md files in git, proposer/critic/tutor agents, React Flow curation UI, Cytoscape/Sigma learner UI, seeded from Learning Commons or a LightRAG/Graphify ingestion pass.
concepts.overview: This is the survey's proposal for building the missing tool, and it is a suggestion, not a validated design. Content lives in a folder of `concepts/*.md` files. Their frontmatter holds `requires`, `helps`, `objectives`, `sources`, a `status` of proposed or reviewed, and a `confidence`. Three agents work on the content: a proposer, a critic and a tutor (see [Proposer, critic and tutor agents](#c/01M3VX5JTFQXZ1SWMG544948TH)). A [React Flow (xyflow)](#c/01M3VX5JTFSD3KMM3VHWHF88BP) editor provides an accept/reject queue for proposed edges, and git commits record provenance. Learners get [Cytoscape.js](#c/01M3VX5JTFF04PQ6EN5ZP4955B) or Sigma.js with a layered layout, a mastery overlay and a "plan my path to X" feature. Seed data comes from [Learning Commons Knowledge Graph](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G) for K-12 or from a LightRAG/Graphify-style ingestion pass. It serves the goal [Build a curatable learning concept DAG](#c/01M3VX5JTF78GRP2WDSYCSW3TV).

concepts.title: Proposer, critic and tutor agents
concepts.summary: Proposer extracts concepts and edges with citations; critic checks cycles, finds missing prerequisites and verifies evidence; tutor explains and quizzes one node at a time.

overviewProv.quote: proposer (extracts concepts and edges from sources, with citations), critic (checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites, verifies evidence)

concepts.overview: This is the proposed trio of agents in the suggested starting stack. The [proposer](#c/01M3VX5JTFHYFNZ5328F6KDG72) extracts concepts and edges from sources, with citations. The [critic](#c/01M3VX5JTF4QQHKVN1H1FNBJP8) checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites and verifies evidence. The [tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF6J94J0YYCN4XFN9J) writes per-node explanations and quizzes. The division of labor echoes the SyllabusGraph pattern of an independent critic pass, and it puts the tutor downstream of the curated graph, in line with [keeping the graph separate from the tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF). Because LLMs are weak prerequisite judges, the proposer's output is only a proposal until a human reviews it. The agents are meant to be distributed as an agent skill or MCP server.

concepts.title: Curation bottleneck
concepts.summary: Metacademy's downfall: experts had to hand-write every node and edge. LLM-assisted curation targets exactly this.

overviewProv.quote: experts had to hand-write every node and edge. LLM-assisted curation fixes exactly that.

concepts.overview: The curation bottleneck is the risk that killed the original prerequisite-graph systems: expert humans had to hand-write every node and edge, and that does not scale. [Metacademy](#c/01M3VX5JTFXGVR2BJNEK0ZKH28) is the clearest case. It had a clean data model of concepts, prerequisites and curated resources, but it was archived in 2023. The report presents LLM-assisted curation as the fix for exactly this problem, and that motivates [the open slot: a reviewed concept DAG](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P). The LLM proposes and the human reviews, so effort shifts from writing everything to approving. LLMs are unreliable on prerequisites, though, so the review step cannot be dropped.

concepts.title: License traps
concepts.summary: roadmap.sh is personal-use only, AFFiNE is mixed, tldraw needs a commercial license in production, Learning Commons has gated datasets, and AGPL tools (Khoj, Logseq, InfraNodus plugin) constrain reuse. Needs checking before building.

overviewProv.quote: Personal use only, no redistribution or commercial reuse without permission.

concepts.overview: License traps are the places where an attractive tool cannot simply be built on. [roadmap.sh](#c/01M3VX5JTFCR3JQRMANXC178KZ) is one of GitHub's most-starred repos, yet its custom license allows personal use only, so you can study it but not reuse it. AFFiNE has a mixed license, Logseq and the InfraNodus plugin are AGPL-3.0, and Khoj is AGPL-3.0 too, as noted in [Other PKM tools (InfraNodus, Logseq, AFFiNE)](#c/01M3VX5JTF8VPBXXTKZXEDC2AH). tldraw, in [Mind-map and canvas libraries](#c/01M3VX5JTFZVBHPJKN85302YAF), needs a commercial license in production. Learning Commons has some gated datasets. These traps challenge the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC): every component must be license-checked before the build starts.

concepts.title: How to build graphs beyond K-12, code and math?
concepts.summary: Open. Vetted graphs exist for K-12 (Learning Commons), formal math (blueprints) and code (mechanical extraction); general knowledge needs LLM-proposed, human-verified prerequisite edges, and the report gives no validated method.

overviewProv.quote: General knowledge needs LLM-proposed and human-verified prerequisite edges instead.

concepts.overview: This open question asks how to get prerequisite graphs outside the domains where they are already easy or vetted. The report finds three solved cases: K-12 can import the Learning Commons skeleton, formal math has blueprint dependency graphs, and code dependencies can be extracted mechanically, as [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) does. General knowledge has none of these. It needs LLM-proposed, human-verified prerequisite edges, and the report offers no validated method for doing this. That gap tempers [the open slot: reviewed concept DAG](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P): the opening is real, but unvetted domains remain unproven. It is part of the [design implications and build plan](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVF7GHGFB3E991GW).

concepts.title: How to model depth-qualified prerequisites?
concepts.summary: Open. SyllabusGraph hints that a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency needing a calculation; how to combine mastery levels with edge types in practice is unresolved.

overviewProv.quote: Consider *depth-qualified* prerequisites ("requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*")

concepts.overview: This open question asks how to express that a prerequisite is met only at a certain depth, for example "requires B at the apply level, not just define". [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) hints at it with a mastery level in which a definition does not satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation. It follows from [using distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD): once edges are typed as requires, helps and so on, depth adds a second dimension. The report does not say how to combine mastery levels with edge types in practice, so the question is unresolved. It is part of the [design implications and build plan](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVF7GHGFB3E991GW).

concepts.title: Metacademy
concepts.summary: The original "package manager for knowledge": pick a target concept and get all unmet prerequisites in topological order with curated resources. Archived 2023; no LLM; curation bottleneck killed it.

overviewProv.quote: Its downfall was the **curation bottleneck**: experts had to hand-write every node and edge.

concepts.overview: Metacademy was the original "package manager for knowledge", mostly covering machine learning and statistics. You pick a target concept and it computes a personalized learning plan: all unmet prerequisites in topological order, each with curated resources and time estimates. It is the cleanest statement of the Expedition's central idea, and its data model of concept, prerequisites and resources is worth reusing. It was archived in 2023 (688 stars, GPL-3.0 code, CC BY-SA content) and predates LLMs. Its downfall was the [Curation bottleneck](#c/01M3VX5JTFEKMXGWF0CT69D643): experts had to hand-write every node and edge. LLM-assisted curation fixes exactly that problem, which is why Metacademy frames the whole project, and its learning plan is the model for the DAG-first view.

concepts.title: Encompassing edges and implicit credit
concepts.summary: Practicing an advanced topic gives fractional review credit to its prerequisites, weighted by edge weight (Math Academy and the propositional-logic clone).

overviewProv.quote: hand-curated topic graph with "encompassing" edges, so practicing an advanced topic gives implicit review credit to its prerequisites

concepts.overview: Encompassing edges encode the idea that one topic contains another, so practicing the advanced topic also counts as review of the simpler one. [Math Academy](#c/01M3VX5JTFDNTBN42YTX9C9XJT) uses a hand-curated topic graph with such edges, giving implicit review credit to prerequisites and supporting diagnostic placement. The open-source propositional-logic clone does the same, giving fractional credit to prerequisite topics weighted by edge weight across its 29-topic DAG. For this Expedition the idea is an extra edge type in [Use distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD), and it changes the [Mastery model](#c/01M3VX5JTFK0Z1NYA54QC13AYW): credit flows down the graph, so learners review less. It is a proposal here, not a tested feature.

concepts.title: PathFinder (Learning-Path)
concepts.summary: Hand-built, cycle-validated skill DAG (NetworkX) plus LangGraph agents for gap finding, scheduling, quizzes and explanations; Bayesian Knowledge Tracing estimates mastery and replans on quiz scores.

overviewProv.quote: **Bayesian Knowledge Tracing** estimates mastery, and the plan is redone when quiz scores come in.

concepts.overview: PathFinder, published as the Learning-Path repo, is a tiny project (0 stars) worth reading for its design. It combines a hand-built skill DAG in NetworkX, validated for cycles, with LangGraph agents that find gaps, schedule study, and generate quizzes and explanations. Mastery is estimated with [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/01M3VX5JTF73ZNZ625SBW6M4Y8), and the plan is redone whenever quiz scores come in. That makes it a compact example of a transparent mastery model driving a path through a prerequisite graph, which is the learner-state pattern the Expedition recommends copying. Its graph is hand-edited JSON, so curation is only partial, and its visual graph is partial. It illustrates [Best patterns come from tiny projects](#c/01M3VX5JTFB8BRJK63TSVKWP1M): good ideas, not adoption.

concepts.title: OpenMAIC
concepts.summary: Tsinghua multi-agent classroom (AI teacher, TA, classmates) that turns a topic or document into slides, quizzes and simulations. Human-editable outline before generation; a linear outline, not a graph.

overviewProv.quote: A linear course *outline*, not a graph. No prerequisite modeling.

concepts.overview: OpenMAIC, from Tsinghua, turns a topic or document into a multi-agent classroom with an AI teacher, a TA and classmates, producing slides, quizzes, simulations and project-based learning. At about 38.9k stars under MIT, with v1.0 in August 2026, it is one of the two big [AI tutors and course generators](#c/01M3VX5JTFZPDYGDKAV1GBXVBR). Its pipeline goes from outline to scenes, and the outline is human-editable before generation, with "Edit with AI" applying validated JSON-patch edits. That makes it a good reference for human-edits-the-plan-then-agents-generate, and the outline-editing step is the curation hook. Its gap is structural: the outline is linear, not a graph, so it fails both the [prerequisite graph](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z) and [visual exploration](#c/01M3VX5JTETK31MX1A5D8ZDA40) tests.

concepts.title: STORM / Co-STORM
concepts.summary: Stanford OVAL: STORM writes cited Wikipedia-style articles; in Co-STORM a human joins agent discussion while a dynamic mind map serves as shared conceptual space. Best-studied co-exploration design, but a taxonomy not prerequisites; activity slowed.

overviewProv.quote: a hierarchical concept structure that serves as a *shared conceptual space between human and system*.

concepts.overview: STORM, from Stanford OVAL, researches a topic and writes a cited, Wikipedia-style article. In Co-STORM a human joins a discussion among agents, "experts" and a moderator, while the system maintains a dynamic mind map: a hierarchical concept structure that serves as a shared conceptual space between human and system. With about 31.5k stars under MIT, it is the best-studied design for human and LLM co-exploration of a topic, and it clearly meets the need for [human and LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE). Its weakness for this Expedition is the structure itself: a taxonomy, not prerequisites, so it fails the test for a [concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z). It also keeps no learner state, and activity has slowed, with the last push in September 2025.

concepts.title: GraphRAG and agent-memory tools
concepts.summary: Entity/relation graph extractors for retrieval or agent memory: microsoft/graphrag (36k★), LightRAG (39.8k★), Graphiti (31.1k★), Cognee (31k★), Neo4j LLM Graph Builder (5.3k★), knowledge_graph, llmgraph. No pedagogy and noisy for teaching, but usable as an ingestion layer.

overviewProv.quote: They could serve as the ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts in a corpus.

concepts.overview: This group covers GraphRAG and agent-memory infrastructure: microsoft/graphrag (36k stars), LightRAG (39.8k), Graphiti (31.1k), Cognee (31k), Neo4j LLM Graph Builder (5.3k), knowledge_graph and llmgraph. They extract entity and relation graphs from text for retrieval or memory, so they are a useful substrate but not pedagogy. They do not model "learn A before B", their graphs are noisy for teaching, and they fail [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z). They could still serve as the ingestion layer that finds candidate concepts in a corpus, and the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC) names a LightRAG-style pass for seed data. [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) uses LightRAG inside its retrieval.

concepts.title: Obsidian + Breadcrumbs
concepts.summary: Breadcrumbs adds typed, directed links (e.g. requires) from frontmatter and builds a real directed graph in Obsidian. Combined with the LLM Wiki pattern, a working prerequisite-graph prototype today.

overviewProv.quote: Combine it with the LLM Wiki pattern to get a working prerequisite-graph prototype today.

concepts.overview: Obsidian with the Breadcrumbs plugin is the most practical do-it-yourself route to a prerequisite graph. Breadcrumbs reads typed, directed links (up/down/next/prev, or custom ones like `requires`) from note frontmatter and builds a real directed graph. Paired with the LLM Wiki pattern, it gives a working prototype today, the core of the [Weekend DIY prototype](#c/01M3VX5JTFV1MWZTC2B13GNJN7): one note per concept with a `requires:` field, an agent proposing notes and edges, and review through git diffs. Obsidian is closed-source but free, while Breadcrumbs is open source (about 800 stars). The route lacks a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and a shared review workflow, so it meets [Visual exploration](#c/01M3VX5JTETK31MX1A5D8ZDA40) only for the author, not for learners.

concepts.title: Edges are proposals with evidence
concepts.summary: Make every prerequisite edge a proposal carrying a confidence score and cited evidence (SyllabusGraph); route low-confidence or high-impact edges to a human review queue (ACE); record who approved what.

overviewProv.quote: Make every edge a **proposal** that carries a confidence score and cited evidence

concepts.overview: This claim is the central design rule for LLM-built graphs: a prerequisite edge is a proposal, never a fact. Each proposed edge carries a confidence score and cited evidence, a pattern borrowed from SyllabusGraph. Low-confidence or high-impact edges are routed to a human review queue, following the ACE pattern, and the system records who approved what. The reasoning is that prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and errors cost the most, since a missing or backwards prerequisite sends learners into material they cannot yet follow. It rests on [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9) and [ACE (AI-assisted educational KG construction)](#c/01M3VX5JTFBP36DDQ7PBZTN44P), and it is what the [Review queue for proposed edges](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4) puts into practice.

concepts.title: K12-KGraph / K12-Bench
concepts.summary: 2026 curriculum-aligned KG with an LLM extraction pipeline. On prerequisite reasoning Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match.

overviewProv.quote: Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match.

concepts.overview: K12-KGraph, with its K12-Bench benchmark, is a 2026 curriculum-aligned knowledge graph built with an LLM extraction pipeline. Its importance here is the measurement. On prerequisite reasoning, Gemini-3-Flash reaches 57% exact match and Gemma-4-31B 46%. These are the numbers behind the claim that [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9). That claim justifies the Expedition's central design choice: treat LLM-proposed prerequisite edges as proposals needing human review, not as facts. It sits in the [research evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTFGD8A9DWXNX54Q2FJ) alongside ACE, which supplies the review-queue blueprint that answers this weakness.

concepts.title: ACE (AI-assisted educational KG construction)
concepts.summary: JEDM 2024: scores concept pairs, sends top-ranked candidates to experts and infers further edges from what they confirm. Big cut in expert effort; students following ACE's order did better. The blueprint for a review queue.

overviewProv.quote: Scores concept pairs, sends the top-ranked candidates to experts, and infers more edges from what experts confirm.

concepts.overview: ACE, published in the Journal of Educational Data Mining in 2024, is the research paper the Expedition treats as the blueprint for a review queue. It scores concept pairs, sends only the top-ranked candidates to experts, and infers further edges from what the experts confirm. This greatly reduces expert effort, and students who studied in ACE's order had better success rates. Its dataset and code are on GitHub. It matters here because [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9) yet exhaustive expert review is too costly, which was the downfall of hand-curated systems. ACE shows how to route scarce human attention to the highest-value edges, informing the [review queue for proposed edges](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4) and the idea that [edges are proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX).

sections.heading: What does ACE do?
sections.md:
ACE (AI-Assisted Construction of Educational Knowledge Graphs) was published in the *Journal of Educational Data Mining* in 2024. Rather than asking experts to review every possible relation, it works in three steps:

1. It **scores concept pairs** to find likely prerequisite relations.
2. It sends only the **top-ranked candidates** to experts.
3. It **infers further edges** from what the experts confirm.

prov.quote: Scores concept pairs, sends the top-ranked candidates to experts, and infers more edges from what experts confirm.

sections.heading: What did it show?
sections.md:
The reported results are a big cut in expert effort, and students who studied in ACE's order had better success rates. The dataset and code are available on GitHub.

This addresses the problem that sank hand-curated systems such as Metacademy, where experts had to write every node and edge. It also fits the finding that frontier LLMs reach only about 46–57% exact match on prerequisite reasoning in K12-Bench. Human confirmation is needed, but it can be spent where it matters most.

sections.heading: Why is it the blueprint for a review queue?
sections.md: The Sources call ACE the **blueprint for the review queue**. Candidate edges are ranked, the highest-value ones are shown to a person, and each confirmation can imply more edges. Applied to a curatable concept DAG, this means an agent proposes edges with scores and evidence, and the [review queue for proposed edges](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4) shows reviewers the most important ones first. It is the research basis for treating [edges as proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX).

prov.quote: Blueprint for the review queue.

concepts.title: Concept Catalyst
concepts.summary: 2026 work where teachers build concept maps while the LLM stays behind the UI as a suggestion generator, keeping decisions with the teacher.

overviewProv.quote: Teachers build concept maps while the LLM stays behind the UI as a suggestion generator.

concepts.overview: Concept Catalyst is a 2026 research paper in which teachers build concept maps themselves while an LLM stays behind the interface as a suggestion generator. The design keeps decisions with the teacher: the model proposes and the human disposes. That matches the human-in-the-loop pattern this Expedition argues for, and it supports [The open slot: reviewed concept DAG](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P), a tool where an agent proposes and a person reviews. It is one entry in [Research evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTFGD8A9DWXNX54Q2FJ), next to the studies on how unreliable LLM prerequisite judgments are. The report summarizes it in one line and gives no results.

concepts.title: Curation UI
concepts.summary: Editable interface where a human edits the graph and accepts or rejects what agents propose; git commits record provenance.

overviewProv.quote: React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges. Git commits record provenance.

prov.quote: React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges. Git commits record provenance.

concepts.overview: The curation UI is where a person stays in control of what the agents produce. The suggested design is a React Flow editor with an accept/reject queue for proposed edges, and git commits record who approved what. It matters because prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest, and a missing or backwards edge sends learners into material they cannot follow. The interface therefore centres on the [review queue for proposed edges](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4), modelled on the ACE research pattern of sending only the top-ranked candidates to experts. Editing is built on [React Flow (xyflow)](#c/01M3VX5JTFSD3KMM3VHWHF88BP), and the whole UI is one part of the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC). It is separate from the learner-facing view, which is read-oriented.

concepts.title: Learner UI
concepts.summary: Zoomable, layered DAG view for learners with a mastery overlay and "plan my path to X".

overviewProv.quote: Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js with dagre/ELK layered layout, a mastery overlay, and "plan my path to X".

prov.quote: Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js with dagre/ELK layered layout, a mastery overlay, and "plan my path to X".

concepts.overview: The learner UI is the part of the suggested stack that learners actually see. It is a zoomable graph of the concept DAG, built with Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js and a dagre/ELK layered layout, with a mastery overlay and a "plan my path to X" action. It follows the [Visualize DAG-first](#c/01M3VX5JTFX0TSN263GMZ3HA6P) principle: foundations at the bottom, goals above, zoom out to a whole-field map, and mark AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed in a distinct style. The overlay shows state from the [Mastery model](#c/01M3VX5JTFK0Z1NYA54QC13AYW), which this UI contains. It is separate from the curation UI that editors use. Within the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC) it is the learner's window onto the reviewed graph.

concepts.title: Other research on concept and prerequisite extraction
concepts.summary: Graphusion (RAG KG build with global merge), ProPRL (property-aware prerequisite learning), tutor-chat knowledge-gap detection, MDPI study (few-shot beats zero-shot by ~6 points; prerequisites gain most), CourseMapper (bottom-up beat top-down; Wikipedia links), TutorialBank/LectureBank datasets, a 2025 concept-map generation review.

overviewProv.quote: Few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by ~6 points on relation extraction, and prerequisites gain the most from examples.

concepts.overview: This is a cluster of smaller research results on pulling concepts and prerequisite links out of text, listed alongside the headline studies in [Research evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTFGD8A9DWXNX54Q2FJ). Graphusion builds knowledge graphs with RAG and a global merge step. ProPRL learns prerequisite relations using properties of the concepts. Another study maps student questions from tutor chats onto a prerequisite graph to find missing foundations. A 2025 MDPI paper found few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by about 6 points on relation extraction, with prerequisites gaining most. CourseMapper found bottom-up construction beat top-down, and it linked concepts to Wikipedia, which backs [Reuse vetted graphs](#c/01M3VX5JTFTBA6PQJEN5GGYSBG). TutorialBank and LectureBank are hand-labeled datasets for evaluation. The few-shot gain complicates [LLMs are weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9): prompting helps, but the report does not call the result reliable.

concepts.title: No tool does all four
concepts.summary: No open-source project covers prerequisite graph, visual exploration, LLM/agent features and human+LLM co-curation well today; each group covers one or two pillars.

overviewProv.quote: No open-source project does all four well today.

concepts.overview: This is the Expedition's central finding: no open-source project today does all four things asked for, namely a prerequisite graph, visual exploration, built-in LLM capabilities and human+LLM co-curation. The landscape splits into groups that each cover one or two pillars. Prerequisite-graph systems have the right data model but little LLM help. AI tutors such as [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) have huge adoption but no curated prerequisite graph. Code tools like [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) have the right UX, but only for codebases. [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) comes closest but is tiny and only partly curated. The finding answers the guiding question and leads directly to [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P).

sections.heading: What are the four things asked for?
sections.md:
The question was which open-source tools already do most of the following:

1. A **concept graph with prerequisites**: well-defined chunks joined by "you need A before B" edges.
2. **Visual exploration**: seeing where a concept sits, what it depends on and what it unlocks.
3. **Built-in LLM or agent capabilities**: generating nodes, proposing edges, explaining, tutoring and checking mastery.
4. **Human + LLM co-curation**: a person reviews, edits and approves what the LLM proposes, with provenance.

The finding is that no open-source project does all four well.

prov.quote: No open-source project does all four well today.

sections.heading: Where does each group fall short?
sections.md:
The space splits into groups that each cover one or two pillars:

- **Prerequisite-graph learning systems** (Metacademy, Oppia, Learning Commons, small DAG/mastery engines) have the right data model but little or no LLM co-authoring and weak visualization. [Oppia](#c/01M3VX5JTF8TZHMY8D8Y65PFMK) has strong skill chunks and learner state but no concept map. [Learning Commons](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G) is a data layer, not a viewer or editor.
- **AI tutors and course generators** such as [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN) and OpenMAIC have huge adoption but no explicit, curatable prerequisite graph.
- **Graphs that teach for code**, such as [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) and Graphify, show the desired UX, but for codebases, where dependencies can be extracted mechanically.
- **LLM knowledge curation**, such as the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV) and Co-STORM, gives human and LLM a shared structure, but a wiki or mind-map hierarchy and not a prerequisite DAG.
- **GraphRAG infrastructure** extracts entity/relation graphs for retrieval and models no pedagogy.

sections.heading: What is the closest near miss?
sections.md: [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H) comes closest. Its agent pipeline cites evidence for every concept and edge, an independent critic model reviews the graph, and it offers an interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom. But its human audit is still pending and it has 1★. The comparison matrix rates it only partial on human curation and learner state, so it is a near miss and not a counterexample.

sections.heading: How firm is the claim, and what follows?
sections.md: The claim rests on a research snapshot dated 2026-09-24, and several of the projects with the best design ideas are tiny, with 0–1★. Newer tools could already have closed the gap, so this is a judgement about the landscape at that date and not a permanent fact. The Sources' conclusion is that a local-first, git-backed concept DAG, with agent-proposed edges reviewed by a human and a zoomable learner view, is a slot nothing mature and open fills. That is the content of [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P).

concepts.title: LLMs are weak prerequisite judges
concepts.summary: Frontier LLMs reach only ~46–57% exact match on K12-Bench prerequisite reasoning, and a missing or backwards edge sends learners into material they can't follow, so human review is needed.

overviewProv.quote: LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges.

concepts.overview: This claim says that language models alone cannot be trusted to decide what must be learned before what. On K12-Bench prerequisite reasoning, frontier models score only about 46–57% exact match (Gemini-3-Flash 57%, Gemma-4-31B 46%), per the [K12-KGraph benchmark](#c/01M3VX5JTF20PV52WBR4MQQCMR). The stakes are high: a missing or backwards prerequisite sends learners into material they cannot yet follow. The claim is why the Expedition treats [edges as proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX) and why [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P) centers on human review. Other research shows few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by about six points, but the report still treats LLMs as short of reliable.

sections.heading: What does the evidence show?
sections.md:
The main figures come from the K12-KGraph / K12-Bench work (2026), a curriculum-aligned knowledge graph with an LLM extraction pipeline. On the benchmark's prerequisite reasoning task, Gemini-3-Flash reaches **57%** exact match and Gemma-4-31B reaches **46%**. The report's reading is blunt: LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges. See [K12-KGraph / K12-Bench](#c/01M3VX5JTF20PV52WBR4MQQCMR) for the benchmark itself.

The figures describe exact match on a hard judgment task. They don't say LLMs are useless at proposing candidates. They say a model's verdict cannot be accepted without checking.

prov.quote: Gemini-3-Flash scores 57% and Gemma-4-31B 46% exact match. **LLMs alone are not reliable prerequisite judges.**

sections.heading: Why do prerequisite errors cost so much?
sections.md:
The Sources note that prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest and where errors cost the most. A **missing** prerequisite lets a learner skip a foundation. A **backwards** one sends them into material they can't yet follow. Either way the graph misdirects the very person it is meant to guide.

A wrong edge in a learner-facing path is also hard to notice. The learner just sees a path that doesn't work, and may blame themselves rather than the graph.

prov.quote: A missing or backwards prerequisite sends learners into material they can't yet follow.

sections.heading: What follows for how graphs are built?
sections.md:
The Sources draw a design rule from this: make every edge a **proposal** carrying a confidence score and cited evidence, and route low-confidence or high-impact edges to a human review queue, recording who approved what. This is the idea behind [edges as proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX), and it is why [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P) centers on human review.

The research cited for this approach is ACE, a human-in-the-loop method that ranks candidate edges and asks experts to confirm only the top ones. It cut expert effort a lot, and students who followed its learning orders had better success rates.

sections.heading: Do better prompts fix it?
sections.md: Partly. Another study, on educational concept and relation extraction, found few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by about six points, with prerequisites gaining the most from examples (see [other research on concept and prerequisite extraction](#c/01M3VX5JTFY9BC1T1EJY48PH0G)). That is a real improvement, but a gain of that size doesn't turn a 46–57% judge into a reliable one. The report still treats LLMs as proposers whose work needs checking.

prov.quote: Few-shot prompting beats zero-shot by ~6 points on relation extraction, and prerequisites gain the most from examples.

concepts.title: The open slot: reviewed concept DAG
concepts.summary: Nothing mature and open offers a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent proposes nodes and edges with evidence and confidence, humans accept or reject in a review queue, and learners explore with mastery overlays.

overviewProv.quote: Nothing mature and open fills this slot.

concepts.overview: The open slot is the gap the survey leaves: a local-first, git-backed concept DAG where an agent proposes nodes and prerequisite edges with evidence and confidence, a human accepts or rejects them in a review queue, and learners explore a zoomable graph with mastery overlays. The Sources say nothing mature and open fills it.
