It follows from [the finding that no tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV) and rests on [the weakness of LLMs as prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9), which is why review is central. It defines what to build in [the learning concept DAG goal](#c/01M3VX5JTF78GRP2WDSYCSW3TV). It is marked contested, because no validated method yet exists for domains without vetted graphs.

sections.heading: What exactly is missing?
sections.md:
The survey scored many tools against four pillars: a concept graph with prerequisites, visual exploration, built-in LLM/agent capabilities, and human+LLM co-curation. No open-source project does all four well, as [the finding that no tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV) records. The open slot is the specific combination the Sources describe:

- **Local-first and git-backed**: content lives in files the user owns.
- **An agent proposes** nodes and prerequisite edges, with evidence and confidence.
- **A human reviews**: accepting or rejecting proposals in a review queue.
- **Learners explore** a zoomable graph with mastery overlays.

The Sources state that nothing mature and open fills this slot.

prov.quote: Nothing mature and open fills this slot.

sections.heading: Why is review at the center?
sections.md:
The slot rests on [LLMs being weak prerequisite judges](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9). Frontier models get only about 46–57% exact match on prerequisite reasoning, and a wrong edge sends learners into material they can't follow. So the agent's role is to propose, and a person decides.

It also answers the older problem of the [curation bottleneck](#c/01M3VX5JTFEKMXGWF0CT69D643). Metacademy's experts had to hand-write every node and edge. LLM proposals plus human review aim to remove that cost without giving up trust. Concept Catalyst, where teachers build concept maps while the LLM stays behind the interface as a suggestion generator, is cited as supporting this division of labor.

sections.heading: Which existing pieces point toward it?
sections.md:
The Sources name partial models to copy rather than a finished tool:

- [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T) for a typed dependency graph with per-node status and humans and AI working in parallel, though for proofs rather than pedagogy.
- SyllabusGraph for edges that cite evidence plus an independent critic pass.
- ACE for the review queue.
- Understand-Anything for the UX of an LLM-built graph with a dependency-ordered guided tour, though for code.
- Oppia and PathFinder for learner modeling.

The Sources also suggest a starting stack: concept files with `status: proposed|reviewed`, proposer, critic and tutor agents, a React Flow curation UI and a Cytoscape.js or Sigma.js learner view. That is the plan behind [the goal of a curatable learning concept DAG](#c/01M3VX5JTF78GRP2WDSYCSW3TV).

sections.heading: Why is this claim contested?
sections.md: The gap is clear, but how to fill it is not settled. Where vetted graphs exist (K-12 via Learning Commons, formal math via blueprint dependency graphs), they can be reused. For other domains the open question is [how to build graphs beyond K-12, code and math](#c/01M3VX5JTF66JJZ895756M8WN5): there is no validated method, and the tools that show the right user experience, such as Understand-Anything, work where dependencies can be extracted mechanically. So the opening is real, but the work needed to occupy it is largely unproven.

concepts.title: Use distinct edge types
concepts.summary: Useful types: requires (hard prerequisite), helps (soft), part-of, related, encompasses (Math Academy-style implicit practice). Consider depth-qualified prerequisites ("requires B at apply level, not just define").

overviewProv.quote: Consider *depth-qualified* prerequisites ("requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*")

concepts.overview: A bare "requires" link is too blunt for a learning graph, so this idea proposes distinct edge types. Useful ones are `requires` (hard prerequisite), `helps` (soft prerequisite), `part-of` (decomposition), `related`, and `encompasses` (Math Academy-style implicit practice, see [Encompassing edges and implicit credit](#c/01M3VX5JTF78BF5A42144QBYEP)). Skillgraph_OS already separates "prerequisite" from "helps-with" edges. The source also suggests depth-qualified prerequisites, such as requiring B at the apply level and not just define, which SyllabusGraph hints at and which raises [How to model depth-qualified prerequisites?](#c/01M3VX5JTFG9QQFPV5AEK56J2W). These types refine the basic [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z), and they must exist before [Edges are proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX) can work per typed edge.

concepts.title: Plain files plus git beat a database
concepts.summary: One markdown file per concept with frontmatter; every successful curated-knowledge project keeps content in version-controlled files, so agents and humans edit the same files and review happens in diffs or PRs, with CI checks for cycles and dangling references.
concepts.overview: The survey argues that plain files under version control beat a database for curation. The recommended shape is one markdown file per concept, with frontmatter for prerequisites, objectives, resources and checks. The evidence is that every successful curated-knowledge project it reviewed works this way: [roadmap.sh](#c/01M3VX5JTFCR3JQRMANXC178KZ), Learn Anything, [Lean Blueprint](#c/01M3VX5JTF84KCJWATP4RGYX3T), the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV) and the committed JSON graph of [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7). Agents and humans edit the same files, and review happens in diffs or pull requests. CI checks can then catch prerequisite cycles and dangling references, as [OpenScienceBasedLearningPlatform](#c/01M3VX5JTFT71WC90C5DSQF0XV) does. The idea shapes the [Content store (concept files)](#c/01M3VX5JTFFTN1XFMYPDCBYEWH) and underpins [Human + LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE).

concepts.title: Keep graph separate from tutor
concepts.summary: The curated DAG decides what to learn and in what order; an LLM tutor handles how, one node at a time. Mastery should come from a transparent model (BKT or Math Academy-style credit), not LLM judgment.

overviewProv.quote: Mastery should come from a transparent model (BKT, or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites), not from LLM judgment.

concepts.overview: This design principle splits two jobs that are easy to blur. The curated prerequisite DAG decides what to learn and in what order. An LLM tutor decides how, generating explanations and quizzes for one node at a time. Mastery then comes from a transparent model such as [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/01M3VX5JTF73ZNZ625SBW6M4Y8), or Math Academy-style credit flowing to prerequisites, rather than from the LLM's own judgment. The reason is the research finding that LLMs are unreliable prerequisite judges, so the sequencing should rest on reviewed edges and an auditable model. The separation also lets you reuse existing tutors: the research suggests pairing the DAG with [DeepTutor](#c/01M3VX5JTF60YDP2CVEMYGB4HN)-style agents. In the build plan, the [Tutor agent](#c/01M3VX5JTF6J94J0YYCN4XFN9J) only teaches nodes the graph selects.

concepts.title: Visualize DAG-first
concepts.summary: Prerequisite graphs are DAGs, not trees: a layered (Sugiyama) layout with foundations at the bottom beats force-directed layouts. Show a plan for one target, zoomable to a whole-field map, with mastery overlay and distinct styling for unreviewed AI-proposed edges.

overviewProv.quote: Prerequisite graphs are **DAGs, not trees**.

concepts.overview: Visualize DAG-first is the proposal that a learner-facing view should treat prerequisites as what they are: directed acyclic graphs, not trees. A layered (Sugiyama) layout, with foundations at the bottom and goals at the top, answers "what do I need first?" far better than a force-directed layout. The view should show a plan for one target concept, in the manner of Metacademy's learning plan, and zoom out to a whole-field map. It should overlay mastery and style AI-proposed edges that haven't been reviewed in a distinct way. [Cytoscape.js](#c/01M3VX5JTFF04PQ6EN5ZP4955B) offers dagre and klay layered layouts, and [Sigma.js](#c/01M3VX5JTE8Y75GAH3M40GXHRZ) handles whole-field scale. Tree-shaped [mind-map libraries](#c/01M3VX5JTFZVBHPJKN85302YAF) are easy LLM targets but cannot express a DAG. This idea shapes the [Learner UI](#c/01M3VX5JTFZ2CY342V64RXMGR8).

concepts.title: Reuse vetted graphs
concepts.summary: Where vetted graphs exist, import rather than regenerate: Learning Commons for K-12, Mathlib/blueprint graphs for formal math, Wikipedia/Wikidata to anchor concept identity (as CourseMapper does).

overviewProv.quote: Reuse, don't regenerate, where vetted graphs exist.

concepts.overview: Reuse vetted graphs is the design idea that where a reviewed graph already exists, you import it instead of asking an LLM to regenerate it. For K-12, the [Learning Commons Knowledge Graph](#c/01M3VX5JTF17CKF8H0WJTK8P0G) supplies standards, learning components and progressions, with an MCP server agents can call. Formal math has Mathlib and blueprint dependency graphs. Wikipedia and Wikidata can anchor concept identity, as CourseMapper does in [Other research on concept and prerequisite extraction](#c/01M3VX5JTFY9BC1T1EJY48PH0G). This matters because prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest, so a vetted skeleton gives better [Seed data](#c/01M3VX5JTFP7Z93CV1W54KD36J) and saves curation effort. It still needs a [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z) to import into.

concepts.title: Ship as agent skill or MCP
concepts.summary: Graphify and Understand-Anything reached massive adoption by shipping as skills for Claude Code/Codex/Cursor; a "curate a concept graph" skill plus a static viewer is a low-friction way in.

overviewProv.quote: Graphify and Understand-Anything reached massive adoption by shipping as skills for Claude Code / Codex / Cursor.

concepts.overview: The report's seventh design implication is about distribution rather than architecture: ship the work as an agent skill or MCP server rather than a standalone app. The evidence is adoption. [Graphify](#c/01M3VX5JTFDRBN32X7KNR8FXDD) (~121k★) and [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) (~84k★) both reached massive scale by shipping as skills for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. For this Expedition that means a "curate a concept graph" skill paired with a static viewer is a low-friction way in. It would carry the [proposer, critic and tutor agents](#c/01M3VX5JTFQXZ1SWMG544948TH) to where users already work. It belongs to the wider [design implications and build plan](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVF7GHGFB3E991GW).

concepts.title: Weekend DIY prototype
concepts.summary: About 70% of the vision for a single user: one note per concept with a requires: field, an agent proposing notes and edges reviewed via git diffs, and a Breadcrumbs or Juggl view. Lacks a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and shared review.

overviewProv.quote: You could get ~70% of the vision in a weekend, for a single user

concepts.overview: The weekend prototype is the report's claim that a single user can get roughly 70% of the vision in a couple of days, with no new software. You keep one note per concept, each with a `requires:` field. An agent proposes notes and edges, and you review them as git diffs. A Breadcrumbs or Juggl view draws the result. It works because it combines two existing pieces: [Obsidian + Breadcrumbs](#c/01M3VX5JTFVVR82GYYSAK21HNY), which turns frontmatter into typed directed links, and the [LLM Wiki pattern](#c/01M3VX5JTFF82BC4F90EBYFKJV), in which an agent maintains plain files. The claim is a proposal, not a tested result. It also names what is missing: a learner-facing view, mastery tracking and a shared review workflow. That is why it sits under [Infrastructure & DIY tooling](#c/01M3VX5JTF9H6P45YCX9PC1WGF) as a way to start, not an endpoint.

concepts.title: Best patterns come from tiny projects
concepts.summary: SyllabusGraph, PathFinder and similar have 0–1★ and unaudited designs; they are sources of ideas, not proven platforms. Star counts are a snapshot from 2026-09-24.

overviewProv.quote: All are tiny (0–1★). They are worth reading for design ideas, not for adoption.

concepts.overview: This risk is a caveat on the Expedition's own evidence. The best design patterns for evidence-backed edges, mastery tracking and cycle checking come from tiny projects with 0–1★: [SyllabusGraph](#c/01M3VX5JTF9JVRPCCY309B402H), [PathFinder (Learning-Path)](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S) and the group in [Other small DAG and mastery engines](#c/01M3VX5JTFPBX8H7MSNH124PXH). The source says they are worth reading for design ideas, not for adoption. Their designs are unaudited and no one has proven them at scale, so they should be copied as patterns, not trusted as platforms. It also weakens [No tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV): that verdict rests on a snapshot taken on 2026-09-24, and newer tools could already close the gap.

concepts.title: Oppia
concepts.summary: Nonprofit open-source lesson platform whose base unit is a skill (concept card, worked examples, misconceptions); lessons declare prerequisite skills. No learner-facing concept map and no LLM authoring.

overviewProv.quote: A proven, battle-tested *granularity*: a skill is phrased as "given X, compute Y", with misconceptions attached.

concepts.overview: Oppia is a free, nonprofit, open-source lesson platform (about 6.8k stars, Apache-2.0, very active) and the most proven example of well-defined learning chunks in this Expedition. Its base unit is a skill, which bundles a concept card, worked examples and misconceptions, and is phrased as "given X, compute Y". Lessons declare prerequisite skills, and those drive review questions at the start of a lesson, so it partly meets [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z). It also meets [Learner state](#c/01M3VX5JTEDCGXQKK50HVQ13QK) and offers creator tools for curation. Its weaknesses are no learner-facing concept map and no LLM authoring of the graph. Its permissive license makes it a [Buildable license](#c/01M3VX5JTFP4W4JWDEP8ET8PEM) model for [Chunked nodes](#c/01M3VX5JTF7GMZBF7H9N2DCAEA).

concepts.title: Learning Commons Knowledge Graph
concepts.summary: Open K-12 prerequisite data from CZI with Anthropic: standards, Learning Components, Learning Progressions, Math Coherence Map, curriculum dependency endpoint; via REST, MCP server and JSONL. A data layer, not a viewer or editor.

overviewProv.quote: For K-12 you can *import* a vetted prerequisite skeleton instead of generating one.

concepts.overview: The Learning Commons Knowledge Graph, from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with Anthropic, is open K-12 prerequisite data, not an application. It bundles US standards from all 50 states, granular Learning Components, Learning Progressions showing how standards build on each other, the Math Coherence Map, aligned curricula, and a curriculum dependency endpoint. Agents and developers reach it through a REST API, an MCP server, JSONL downloads, or plugins for ChatGPT and Claude. Licensing is mixed: many datasets are CC BY 4.0 or CC0, some are gated. Its value here is [Reuse vetted graphs](#c/01M3VX5JTFTBA6PQJEN5GGYSBG): for K-12 you can import an expert-authored prerequisite skeleton instead of generating one, and it is the proposed seed in the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC). It offers no viewer, editor or learner state.

attributes.license: Mixed: many CC BY 4.0 / CC0, some gated

concepts.title: Lean Blueprint
concepts.summary: Typed dependency graph of definitions, lemmas and theorems (\uses{}), with per-node status shown as colors. Small, locally specified nodes let humans and AI work in parallel; progress is a roll-up of statuses. LeanArchitect infers dependencies from Lean code.

overviewProv.quote: Small, locally specified nodes let many humans and AI agents work in parallel

concepts.overview: Lean Blueprint (leanblueprint, with LeanArchitect) is a typed dependency graph of definitions, lemmas and theorems used by major formalization projects (376★, Apache-2.0). `\uses{}` records dependencies, with a statement and its proof carrying separate lists. Each node has a status (not ready, ready, formalized), shown as colors in the rendered graph, and LeanArchitect infers dependencies from Lean code. The Sources call it the best human+AI curation model: small, locally specified nodes let many people and agents work in parallel, and global progress is a roll-up of node statuses. It also keeps data in files, supporting [plain files plus git](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE). It targets proofs rather than pedagogy, so it informs [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P) as a pattern, not a finished answer.

sections.heading: How does a blueprint work?
sections.md:
A blueprint is a typed dependency graph of definitions, lemmas and theorems from a formalization project.

- `\uses{}` records dependencies. A statement and its proof carry **separate** dependency lists.
- Each node has a **status**: not ready, ready, or formalized. The rendered dependency graph shows these as colors.
- **LeanArchitect** (ITP 2026) extracts blueprint data from Lean code and infers dependencies automatically, so the graph doesn't have to be maintained entirely by hand.

leanblueprint has 376★ under Apache-2.0 and is used by major formalization projects. Lean Atlas and TheoremGraph push the idea further toward human-AI collaboration.

sections.heading: Why is it the best curation model in the survey?
sections.md:
The key property is that nodes are small and locally specified. Many humans and AI agents can then work on different nodes in parallel without needing to understand the whole project, and global progress is just a roll-up of node statuses. The Sources call this the collaboration pattern the Expedition wants, applied to proofs instead of pedagogy.

In the survey's comparison it scores strongly on a prerequisite model, chunked nodes, a visual dependency graph and human curation, and partially on LLM capabilities and learner state, where node status stands in for mastery. Those ratings map to the criteria [Concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z), [Chunked nodes](#c/01M3VX5JTF7GMZBF7H9N2DCAEA) and [Human + LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE).

prov.quote: Small, locally specified nodes let many humans and AI agents work in parallel, and global progress is just a roll-up of node statuses.

sections.heading: What should be copied, and what not?
sections.md:
Worth copying are the typed dependencies, per-node status shown visually, small self-contained nodes, and content kept in files. That last point backs [plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE), which lists Lean Blueprint among the successful curated-knowledge projects that keep content under version control.

What it does not do is teach. Its domain is formal proofs, where a dependency is a logical fact that can be inferred from code. A learning graph needs pedagogical prerequisites, which are judgment calls and where [LLMs are weak](#c/01M3VX5JTF1357C8RV4BDN9KN9). That is why it supports [the open slot](#c/01M3VX5JTF788DN1Y4Z1E6CA1P) as a pattern rather than filling it.

concepts.title: SyllabusGraph
concepts.summary: Source-to-course agent pipeline: every concept and edge cites evidence, an independent critic model reviews the graph, interactive zoomable concept map, mastery levels. Demo: 3 QFT books → 117 concepts. Tiny project; human audit pending.

overviewProv.quote: a definition doesn't satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation

concepts.overview: SyllabusGraph is a small MIT-licensed project (1★, active September 2026) that runs a source-to-course agent pipeline through Claude Code or Codex. Every concept and edge cites evidence from the source texts, and an independent critic model reviews the graph. It presents an interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom and has a notion of mastery level: a definition does not satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation. Its demo turned three QFT books into 117 concepts. It comes closest to meeting all four pillars, so it is a pattern for [edges as proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX), but human audit is still pending and it has almost no adoption. It also [raises the question of depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTFG9QQFPV5AEK56J2W).

sections.heading: How does the pipeline work?
sections.md:
SyllabusGraph is a source-to-course agent pipeline. It reads source texts and proposes a concept graph, and it runs through Claude Code or Codex. Two design choices set it apart from most LLM graph builders:

- **Evidence on every item.** Every concept and every edge cites evidence from the source texts, so a reviewer can check a claim against the passage behind it.
- **An independent critic.** A separate critic model reviews the graph, so the model that proposed an edge is not the only one to judge it.

The demo turned three quantum field theory (QFT) books into a graph of 117 concepts.

prov.quote: Every concept and edge cites **evidence** from the source texts, and an **independent critic model** reviews the graph.

sections.heading: What does the learner see, and what is mastery here?
sections.md:
The learner gets an interactive concept map with overview-to-detail zoom. That covers the "where does this sit?" part of visual exploration, going from a whole-field view down to one concept.

SyllabusGraph also has a notion of **mastery level** on dependencies. In the project's words, a definition does not satisfy a dependency that needs a calculation. So a prerequisite can be met at one depth and still be unmet at a deeper one. This is why it [raises the question of depth-qualified prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTFG9QQFPV5AEK56J2W): the Sources suggest an edge such as "requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*". Its learner state is only partial, a mastery level on dependencies rather than a full tracking model.

prov.quote: Consider *depth-qualified* prerequisites ("requires B at the *apply* level, not just *define*"), which SyllabusGraph hints at.

sections.heading: Why does it matter to this Expedition?
sections.md:
The Expedition's central finding is that [no tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV) of the things it asks for. In the comparison matrix SyllabusGraph scores strongly on the prerequisite model, chunked nodes, visualization and LLM/agent support. It is only partial on human curation (human audit is pending) and on learner state. That makes it the closest near miss, not a counterexample.

Its value is as a pattern. The Sources' design implications cite it for making every edge a proposal that carries a confidence score and cited evidence, with low-confidence or high-impact edges routed to a human review queue. That fits the [edges as proposals with evidence](#c/01M3VX5JTF2SW2VN5GHSYWH5WX) idea. This matters because LLMs alone are weak prerequisite judges, so a proposed edge needs evidence and a second opinion.

prov.quote: Make every edge a **proposal** that carries a confidence score and cited evidence (the SyllabusGraph pattern).

sections.heading: What are its limits?
sections.md: SyllabusGraph is tiny: 1★, MIT-licensed, active in September 2026. The Sources group it with other small prerequisite-graph and mastery engines (0–1★) that are "worth reading for design ideas, not for adoption". It therefore fails the adoption and health criterion. The human audit step is still pending, so co-curation is only partly met. The project is a source of patterns, not a platform to build on directly.

prov.quote: All are tiny (0–1★). They are worth reading for design ideas, not for adoption.

concepts.title: roadmap.sh
concepts.summary: Interactive node-based developer roadmaps; each node is a markdown file edited via community PRs. Proves demand and that node-per-file plus PRs scale. Edges are roadmap order, AI features are not in the open repo, and the license is restrictive.

overviewProv.quote: Also proves node-per-file plus PR curation works at scale.

concepts.overview: roadmap.sh (the developer-roadmap repo, about 368k stars) offers interactive node-based roadmaps for developer roles. Each node's content is a markdown file named `content/<topic>@<node-id>.md`, edited through community pull requests. It proves the demand for "show me the map, then let me click a node to learn", and it shows that node-per-file plus PR curation works at scale, which supports [Plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE). Its edges express roadmap order rather than strict prerequisites, and the AI roadmap generator and tutor live on the hosted site, not in the open repo. Its custom restrictive license (personal use only) makes it a clear case of [License traps](#c/01M3VX5JTFD490GQFTHTSJ20XE): you can study it but not build on it.

concepts.title: DeepTutor
concepts.summary: HKU agent-native learning workspace: RAG over your materials, tutoring chat, quizzes, interactive books, mastery paths with progression gates, 3-layer learner memory. Graphs only inside retrieval; no curated prerequisite graph.

overviewProv.quote: You could pair it with a curated concept DAG: the graph decides *what's next*, and DeepTutor-style agents *teach it*.

concepts.overview: DeepTutor, from HKU's Data Science Lab, is the strongest open-source "LLM tutor" foundation in this Expedition: about 40k stars, Apache-2.0, and releases every few days. It is an agent-native workspace that runs retrieval over your own materials, then tutors in chat, solves problems, generates quizzes and "interactive books", and keeps three layers of learner memory. It even offers mastery paths with progression gates, so it covers [Learner state](#c/01M3VX5JTEDCGXQKK50HVQ13QK) well. Its gap is the one that matters here: knowledge graphs appear only inside retrieval (it builds on [GraphRAG and agent-memory tools](#c/01M3VX5JTFZB7W8YXQQ7YNGGC9)), with no curated, learner-visible prerequisite graph. That is why it supports [Keep graph separate from tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF): a curated DAG decides what comes next, and DeepTutor-style agents teach it.

concepts.title: Understand-Anything
concepts.summary: Multi-agent pipeline (scanner, analyzers, tour-builder, graph-reviewer) that turns a codebase into an interactive knowledge graph with dependency-ordered guided tours; graph committed as JSON. "Graphs that teach > graphs that impress." The product shape wanted, but for code.

overviewProv.quote: Graphs that teach > graphs that impress.

concepts.overview: Understand-Anything is a roughly 84k-star, MIT-licensed tool in which a multi-agent pipeline (scanner, file and architecture analyzers, tour-builder, graph-reviewer) turns a codebase into an interactive force-directed knowledge graph. It offers semantic search, Q&A, and guided tours ordered by dependency. The graph is committed as JSON so teams share it, and a read-only viewer needs no LLM. The Sources call it the product shape the Expedition wants, with a tagline "Graphs that teach > graphs that impress". Its limit is its domain: code dependencies can be extracted mechanically, whereas general knowledge needs LLM-proposed, human-verified edges, which is why it also [raises the question of building beyond code](#c/01M3VX5JTF66JJZ895756M8WN5). Its separate reviewer agent and committed JSON are worth copying, and it has no learner state.

sections.heading: How does it turn a codebase into a graph?
sections.md:
Understand-Anything (about 84k★, MIT) is a multi-agent pipeline made of a scanner, file and architecture analyzers, a **tour-builder** and a **graph-reviewer**. Together they turn a codebase into an interactive force-directed knowledge graph. On top of that graph it offers:

- semantic search and Q&A over the graph;
- **guided tours** that walk through the architecture in dependency order.

The graph is committed as JSON so teams share it, and a read-only viewer needs no LLM.

prov.quote: **"Guided tours" that walk through the architecture ordered by dependency.**

sections.heading: Why is it the reference for "graphs that teach"?
sections.md:
Its tagline is "Graphs that teach > graphs that impress." The Sources call it the shape of the product the Expedition wants: an LLM builds a graph, then gives the learner a dependency-ordered tour of it. It also helps that it reached huge adoption, as did Graphify, by shipping as an agent skill. That supports the idea to [ship as an agent skill or MCP](#c/01M3VX5JTF93Z01KF6TF8BA8GB).

The committed JSON graph also backs the case that [plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE) for curation: the graph lives in version control, and agents and humans share it.

prov.quote: Graphs that teach > graphs that impress.

sections.heading: Why doesn't it solve the whole problem?
sections.md:
Its domain is code, where dependencies can be extracted mechanically. General knowledge has no such parser, so prerequisite edges must be proposed by an LLM and verified by a person. That gap is the open question of [how to build graphs beyond K-12, code and math](#c/01M3VX5JTF66JJZ895756M8WN5).

It also has no learner state. In the comparison matrix, learner state is "none" and human curation only partial (via the committed JSON). So it fits the finding that [no tool does all four](#c/01M3VX5JTFYBCPDX9FK0HJNJKV): it has the product shape but only for code.

prov.quote: General knowledge needs LLM-proposed and human-verified prerequisite edges instead.

sections.heading: What should be copied from it?
sections.md:
The Sources single out two features to reuse:

- **A separate graph-reviewer agent.** It parallels the critic in the proposer/critic/tutor design and keeps review independent of generation.
- **A committed JSON graph.** It makes the result shareable and diffable, and lets a viewer run without any LLM.

They also use it as the UX reference for "LLM builds a graph, then gives a guided tour".

prov.quote: The separate **graph-reviewer agent** and the **committed JSON graph** are both worth copying.

concepts.title: Graphify
concepts.summary: A /graphify skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor that turns any folder into a local queryable knowledge graph with explained edges and no Neo4j. Validates "agent skill + local graph file" distribution; edges are relations, not pedagogy.

overviewProv.quote: Validates "agent skill + local graph file + explained edges" as a distribution model.

concepts.overview: Graphify is a `/graphify` skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar agents that turns any folder (code, docs, PDFs, images, video) into a local, queryable knowledge graph. It parses code deterministically through the AST where it can, explains every edge, and needs no Neo4j or vector store. At roughly 121k stars under Apache-2.0 it is the most adopted tool in this Expedition, and it matters mainly as proof of a distribution model: an agent skill plus a local graph file plus explained edges. That is the shape recommended in [Ship as agent skill or MCP](#c/01M3VX5JTF93Z01KF6TF8BA8GB). Its limits are just as instructive. Its edges are general relations, not pedagogy, so it only partly meets the need for a [concept graph with prerequisites](#c/01M3VX5JTEYQTGJ2KQJF8HT56Z), and it tracks no [learner state](#c/01M3VX5JTEDCGXQKK50HVQ13QK). It sits beside [Understand-Anything](#c/01M3VX5JTF4X3DD8GCWH0DMVN7) in the family of LLM-built graphs.

concepts.title: LLM Wiki pattern
concepts.summary: Karpathy's April 2026 pattern: raw/ immutable sources, wiki/ LLM-written interlinked markdown, a schema file (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) governing the agent; human edits in Obsidian. Most popular human+LLM curation workflow; add typed prerequisites: frontmatter to get most of a concept DAG.
concepts.overview: The LLM Wiki is not a product but an influential pattern that Karpathy described in April 2026. A `raw/` folder holds immutable sources and a `wiki/` folder holds interlinked markdown pages written by an LLM. A schema file (`CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`) governs the agent. The human reads and edits in Obsidian while the agent keeps the wiki current. The survey calls it the most popular human+LLM curation workflow right now, and it is a direct example of [Plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE) in practice. Its weakness is that it has only links, with no typed prerequisites and no learner state. The suggested fix is to add typed `prerequisites:` frontmatter, which gets you most of the way to a curatable concept DAG. That makes it the base of the [Weekend DIY prototype](#c/01M3VX5JTFV1MWZTC2B13GNJN7) and a template for [Human + LLM co-curation](#c/01M3VX5JTFNAQPT0M91VN9X3QE).

concepts.title: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
concepts.summary: A transparent probabilistic model of learner mastery, used by PathFinder to estimate mastery and replan when quiz scores arrive.

overviewProv.quote: **Bayesian Knowledge Tracing** estimates mastery, and the plan is redone when quiz scores come in.

concepts.overview: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) is a probabilistic model that estimates how likely a learner is to have mastered a skill, updating that estimate as they answer questions. In this Expedition it appears in [PathFinder](#c/01M3VX5JTFHB5GXVH49PZEN75S), which uses BKT to estimate mastery and redoes the plan when quiz scores arrive. It matters because the design guidance wants mastery to come from a transparent model rather than LLM judgment; this is what allows the tutor to stay [separate from the graph](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF). BKT is one concrete way to build the [mastery model](#c/01M3VX5JTFK0Z1NYA54QC13AYW) and to supply the learner state that most prerequisite tools lack. The alternative named alongside it is Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites.

concepts.title: Content store (concept files)
concepts.summary: A folder of concepts/*.md files; frontmatter holds requires, helps, objectives, sources, status (proposed|reviewed) and confidence.

overviewProv.quote: a folder of `concepts/*.md` files. Frontmatter holds `requires`, `helps`, `objectives`, `sources`

prov.quote: a folder of `concepts/*.md` files. Frontmatter holds `requires`, `helps`, `objectives`, `sources`

concepts.overview: The content store is the suggested starting stack's answer to "where does the knowledge live?": a folder of `concepts/*.md` files, one per concept. Frontmatter carries the structure: `requires` and `helps` for prerequisite edges, plus `objectives`, `sources`, a `status` of proposed or reviewed, and a `confidence` value. This makes each edge a reviewable proposal with provenance, and it lets humans and agents edit the same files. It rests on the principle that [plain files plus git beat a database](#c/01M3VX5JTF7J8YEXMR48QV86SE), because review happens in diffs or PRs and CI can check for cycles and dangling references. The edge vocabulary comes from [using distinct edge types](#c/01M3VX5JTFVDHQY9JDCFWNJFVD). It is the first layer of the [suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC).

concepts.title: Seed data
concepts.summary: Where the first concepts and edges come from: Learning Commons (K-12) or a user corpus through a LightRAG/Graphify-style ingestion pass.

overviewProv.quote: Learning Commons (K-12), or a user corpus through a LightRAG/Graphify-style ingestion pass.

prov.quote: Learning Commons (K-12), or a user corpus through a LightRAG/Graphify-style ingestion pass.

concepts.overview: Seed data is the starting material that fills a concept graph before any agent or human has proposed anything. The suggested stack names two routes. For K-12, import the vetted prerequisite skeleton from Learning Commons. For any other subject, run a user corpus through a LightRAG- or Graphify-style ingestion pass, which finds candidate concepts that agents and reviewers then refine. Both routes follow the advice to [reuse vetted graphs](#c/01M3VX5JTFTBA6PQJEN5GGYSBG) where they exist rather than regenerate them. Seed data matters because it shapes how much work lands on the curation step: a vetted import arrives mostly trustworthy, while an extracted corpus arrives as proposals needing review. It is one part of the [Suggested starting stack](#c/01M3VX5JTF19QWJ566B0MHTBGC).

concepts.title: Mastery model
concepts.summary: Learner state driving the mastery overlay and next-step plan; should be a transparent model, not LLM judgment.

overviewProv.quote: Mastery should come from a transparent model (BKT, or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites)

prov.quote: Mastery should come from a transparent model (BKT, or Math Academy-style credit that flows to prerequisites)

concepts.overview: The mastery model is the learner-state component of the [Learner UI](#c/01M3VX5JTFZ2CY342V64RXMGR8). It drives the mastery overlay on the graph and the "plan my path" next-step suggestions. The report's key rule is that mastery should come from a transparent model, not from LLM judgment. Two candidates are named: [Bayesian Knowledge Tracing](#c/01M3VX5JTF73ZNZ625SBW6M4Y8), used by PathFinder, and Math Academy-style credit in which practice on advanced topics flows to their prerequisites, described under [encompassing edges and implicit credit](#c/01M3VX5JTF78BF5A42144QBYEP). This keeps the curated graph deciding what comes next, while tutor agents handle only how to teach it.

concepts.title: Proposer agent
concepts.summary: Extracts concepts and prerequisite edges from sources, with citations.

overviewProv.quote: proposer (extracts concepts and edges from sources, with citations)

prov.quote: proposer (extracts concepts and edges from sources, with citations)

concepts.overview: The proposer agent is the first step in the suggested pipeline: it reads sources and extracts concepts and prerequisite edges, attaching citations to each. Its output is treated as a proposal, not a fact, carrying a confidence score and cited evidence, which is the SyllabusGraph pattern. That framing matters because prerequisite edges are where LLMs are weakest, so everything it writes must be checked. The [critic agent](#c/01M3VX5JTF4QQHKVN1H1FNBJP8) reviews its work next, and uncertain or high-impact edges go to a human review queue. Together with the tutor, they form [Proposer, critic and tutor agents](#c/01M3VX5JTFQXZ1SWMG544948TH). Seeding can come from vetted graphs or an ingestion pass over a corpus.

concepts.title: Critic agent
concepts.summary: Checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites and verifies the cited evidence.

overviewProv.quote: critic (checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites, verifies evidence)

prov.quote: critic (checks for cycles, finds missing prerequisites, verifies evidence)

concepts.overview: The critic agent is the second reviewer in the proposed pipeline, checking what the [proposer agent](#c/01M3VX5JTFHYFNZ5328F6KDG72) produces before a human sees it. Its jobs are to check for cycles, find missing prerequisites and verify that the cited evidence supports each edge. The design borrows from SyllabusGraph, where an independent critic model reviews the graph, and from Understand-Anything, which has a separate graph-reviewer agent. Separating the critic from the proposer matters because prerequisite reasoning is unreliable for LLMs, so a second pass catches errors cheaply and shortens the human [review queue](#c/01M3VX5JTFTDH5GZ8C5CEZRTH4). It is one of the three roles in [Proposer, critic and tutor agents](#c/01M3VX5JTFQXZ1SWMG544948TH).

concepts.title: Tutor agent
concepts.summary: Writes per-node explanations and quizzes, one node at a time, for the nodes the DAG selects.

overviewProv.quote: tutor (per-node explanation and quizzes)

prov.quote: tutor (per-node explanation and quizzes)

concepts.overview: The tutor agent is the third agent in the suggested stack. It writes explanations and quizzes for a single node at a time, covering whichever nodes the concept DAG selects. It handles *how* to teach, while the graph decides *what* comes next. That division is the point of [Keep graph separate from tutor](#c/01M3VX5JTFGH6RDGTBS8ETHZYF). Mastery should come from a transparent model, not from the tutor's own judgment. The report points to DeepTutor and OpenMAIC as reference designs for this role. It is one of the [Proposer, critic and tutor agents](#c/01M3VX5JTFQXZ1SWMG544948TH).
